items.x: Humanistic psychology grew as a response to what its founders saw as the pessimism of psychoanalysis and the mechanical view of behaviorism. It puts human potential, growth, and self-determination at the center. Maslow's hierarchy of needs Level Need Examples 5 (top) Self-actualization Fulfilling your potential; living in line with your deepest values. 4 Esteem Achievement, competence, recognition, respect. 3 Belonging and love Friendship, closeness, family, connection. 2 Safety Security, stability, freedom from fear. 1 (base) Physiological Food, water, shelter, sleep, warmth. Motivational sequencing Maslow's key claim is that lower needs generally have to be met well enough before higher needs become strong motivators. He described the hierarchy as an order of priorities rather than a rigid pyramid, even though it is usually drawn as one. Rogers and the self Carl Rogers put the self at the center of his theory. Psychological well-being depends on congruence between a person's self-concept and their actual lived experience. Concept What it means Self-concept Your organized beliefs about who you are: your characteristics, values, and sense of self. Ideal self The person you feel you should be or wish to be, shaped partly by standards you have absorbed. Congruence A match between self-concept and lived experience. Linked to psychological health. Incongruence A gap between self-concept and experience, often produced by rigid conditions of worth. Conditions of worth The conditions under which a person feels accepted. When rigid and imposed from outside, the person hides their real experience to keep approval. Unconditional positive regard Acceptance that does not depend on meeting any standard. Rogers saw it as necessary for genuine growth.

items.s: Trait theory and the Big Five
items.g: Trait theory and the Big Five
items.x: Trait theories ask a more descriptive question: what are the stable dimensions along which people differ, and how can we measure them reliably? The Big Five came out of decades of research on the words people use to describe personality, not from one theorist's clinical observations. Dimension High end Low end Openness Imaginative, curious, drawn to new and complex things. Conventional, prefers the familiar, practical. Conscientiousness Organized, dependable, self-disciplined, goal-directed. Flexible, spontaneous, less driven by long-term goals. Extraversion Sociable, assertive, energetic, seeks social stimulation. Reserved, reflective, comfortable alone. Agreeableness Cooperative, trusting, empathetic, values harmony. Competitive, skeptical, blunt, less focused on harmony. Neuroticism Tends toward negative emotion: anxiety, moodiness, reactivity. Emotionally stable, calm, resilient. The most important caution about the Big Five The Big Five is a taxonomy, not a causal theory. It reliably describes and predicts outcomes such as academic performance, relationship quality, and job success, but it does not explain where these dimensions come from or how they develop. Predicting and explaining are not the same thing. For the why, you need the other three approaches. Traits are fairly stable across life, although conscientiousness and agreeableness tend to rise gradually in adulthood.

items.k: reciprocal determinism | Self-efficacy | mastery experiences | vicarious learning | verbal persuasion | physiological states | Two related ideas | Locus of control | Explanatory style | Keep the three apart
items.x: Bandura argued that you cannot understand personality by looking at the person alone. Personality comes from the ongoing, two-way interaction between the person, their behavior, and their environment. He called this reciprocal determinism . Element What it includes How it shapes the others Person Beliefs, expectations, thinking patterns, self-efficacy, emotional tendencies. Shapes which behaviors are chosen and how situations are interpreted. Behavior The actions the person actually takes. Produces consequences in the environment and changes how the person sees themselves. Environment Physical and social setting, other people's reactions, what the situation demands. Shapes the person's beliefs and decides the consequences of behavior. The key idea is that influence runs in all three directions at once. No single element is simply the cause. A belief shapes behavior, which gets a reaction from the environment, which feeds back and changes the belief, and the cycle continues. Self-efficacy Self-efficacy is your belief in your ability to succeed at a specific task. It is domain-specific, not general self-esteem: you can have high self-efficacy in writing and low self-efficacy in public speaking. It is built from four sources: mastery experiences (succeeding yourself), vicarious learning (watching someone similar succeed), verbal persuasion (encouragement from someone credible), and physiological states (how your body feels during the task). High self-efficacy tends to lead to approaching a task; low self-efficacy tends to lead to avoiding it, even when the skill is there. Two related ideas Locus of control is how much you believe outcomes are controlled by your own actions (internal) or by outside forces such as luck or other people (external). Explanatory style , which you met in Unit 2, is your usual way of explaining why good and bad things happen, from optimistic to pessimistic. Keep the three apart Self-efficacy is a belief about whether you can do a specific task. Locus of control is a belief about who or what controls outcomes in general. Explanatory style is how you explain events after they happen.

Students often think: the Big Five explains where personality differences come from. Actually: the Big Five is a taxonomy. It describes and predicts well, but explaining where traits come from needs the psychodynamic, humanistic, or social-cognitive frameworks. Students often think: self-efficacy and self-esteem are the same thing. Actually: self-efficacy is belief in succeeding at a specific task, while self-esteem is a general sense of your own worth. You can have high self-efficacy in writing and low self-efficacy in public speaking. Students often think: reciprocal determinism means the environment is the real cause and the person just reacts. Actually: Bandura rejects one-way causes. Person, behavior, and environment all shape one another at the same time. Students often think: conditions of worth and unconditional positive regard are the same idea. Actually: conditions of worth make acceptance depend on meeting a standard, which can produce incongruence. Unconditional positive regard is acceptance with no conditions at all.

1. During exam week, a 17-year-old starts sleeping with a stuffed toy from early childhood and sulks when he is asked to help at home. Which defense mechanism does this best fit, and why? Show answer Regression: under stress he goes back to an earlier, less mature pattern of behavior. Like all defense mechanisms, it is unconscious, so he is unlikely to see it as a strategy. 2. According to Rogers, what is the difference between a person's self-concept and their ideal self? Show answer The self-concept is who you believe you are. The ideal self is who you feel you should be or wish to be. Rogers linked psychological health to congruence between the self-concept and actual experience; rigid conditions of worth can widen the gap. 3. Why is the Big Five described as a taxonomy rather than a causal theory? Show answer It sorts and describes personality into five dimensions and predicts outcomes well, but it does not explain where those dimensions come from or how they develop. Explaining origins needs the psychodynamic, humanistic, or social-cognitive approaches. 4. Name the three elements of reciprocal determinism and explain why none of them is treated as the only cause. Show answer Person, behavior, and environment. Each one influences the other two at the same time, so the cycle has no single starting point or single cause.

Knowing that personality has stable dimensions is one thing. Measuring them accurately is much harder. Every method has its own strengths and limits, and every method is open to specific, named biases. Method How it works Key strengths and limits Self-report inventory People answer structured questions about their own thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Quick and easy to give to many people. Limited by social desirability bias and by how well people know themselves. Behavioral observation Watching actual behavior in natural or structured settings and coding it against set criteria. More objective than self-report. Slow, expensive, and limited to the situations observed. Informant reports People who know the participant well rate the participant's personality. Can capture what the participant cannot see or will not admit. Affected by the relationship between rater and participant. Projective tests People respond to ambiguous images such as inkblots, and the answers are read as clues to unconscious concerns. Rooted in psychodynamic theory. Low reliability and questionable validity, but still used by some clinicians. Semi-structured interviews A flexible guide of open questions, with follow-ups based on the answers. Rich, detailed information. Open to interviewer bias and social desirability bias.

items.k: The distinction tested most often | Why this matters beyond Unit 3 | Predicting is not explaining
items.x: Knowing the name and the mechanism of each bias lets you spot it in a scenario, and in your own thinking. Bias What it involves Social desirability bias Answering in ways that make you look good, whether or not the answers are accurate. Confirmation bias Noticing and giving more weight to evidence that supports what you already believe, and downplaying evidence against it. Interviewer bias The interviewer's expectations, tone, or body language accidentally shape the participant's answers. Participant bias Informants answer in ways shaped by their relationship with the person they are rating: loyalty, tact, or wanting to avoid conflict. Observer effect People behave differently when they know they are being watched or studied. The distinction tested most often Participant bias applies to informants describing someone else, and comes from their relationship with that person. Social desirability bias applies to a person describing themselves, and comes from their own self-image. Both paint a more favorable picture, but the source of the distortion is different. Why this matters beyond Unit 3 These biases are not only about personality research. They apply to judging any psychological study, including the research methods from Unit 1. Spotting a bias in a personality scenario uses the same skill as evaluating a research design. Predicting is not explaining A reliable link, such as conscientiousness scores predicting career satisfaction, tells you what tends to happen. On its own it does not explain the mechanism or show cause and effect. Keep this in mind whenever a question gives you a correlation or a prediction to evaluate.

Students often think: participant bias and social desirability bias are the same thing. Actually: social desirability bias is about describing yourself. Participant bias is about an informant describing someone else, shaped by their relationship with that person. Students often think: confirmation bias only affects other people's research. Actually: it applies to how you read your own results too, for example focusing only on memories that fit what you already believe about yourself. Students often think: the observer effect is about questionnaires. Actually: the observer effect is behavior changing because people know they are being watched, so it matters most in observation. For questionnaires, social desirability bias is the closer idea. Students often think: if two methods only correlate moderately, one of them must be wrong. Actually: a moderate correlation is often what you would expect. Both methods can pick up real information while each also carries its own separate biases.

1. Participant bias and social desirability bias both make people look better than they really are. Where does each one come from? Show answer Social desirability bias comes from a person describing themselves and wanting to look good. Participant bias comes from an informant describing someone else, shaped by their relationship with that person. 2. A researcher worries that self-reports of agreeableness will be inflated. Which other method could she use, and what new bias might that method bring in? Show answer Informant reports avoid self-presentation but can bring in participant bias. Behavioral observation is more objective but can bring in the observer effect, because people act differently when watched. Every method trades one weakness for another. 3. Why are projective tests still used by some clinicians despite their low reliability and questionable validity? Show answer They come from the psychodynamic tradition, which holds that important concerns are unconscious and will not show up in direct questions. Some clinicians use them as a starting point for conversation rather than as a precise measurement. 4. What is the difference between predictive validity and explanatory power, and why does it matter when you read a personality study? Show answer Predictive validity means a measure reliably forecasts an outcome. Explanatory power means it tells you why the outcome happens. A study can predict well without explaining anything, so a strong prediction is not proof of cause.

A personality trait is a stable, ordinary pattern. A psychological disorder is a pattern that causes clinically significant distress or impairment. The gap between the two is real, but it is not always wide. The biopsychosocial model says that biological, psychological, and social factors interact to produce or protect against a disorder. The diathesis-stress model is a more structured version of that idea: a disorder develops when two things are present together. Component Definition Diathesis A pre-existing vulnerability, biological (such as a genetic predisposition) or psychological (such as a personality pattern or thinking style), that lowers the threshold for a disorder. It exists before any triggering event. Stressor An event or ongoing condition that triggers the disorder in a vulnerable person. The same stressor may have no clinical effect on someone without the diathesis. The most heavily tested skill in this unit Finding the diathesis and the stressor in an unseen scenario. The diathesis is the long-standing pattern described before the triggering event. The stressor is the specific event or change. A symptom, such as the worry, the lost sleep, or the withdrawal, is neither: it is the outcome the model explains. Do not assume neuroticism is the diathesis just because the disorder involves anxiety. The diathesis must be supported by evidence in the scenario.

Find the one-time, specific event. That is almost always the stressor. Find the long-standing pattern described as existing before that event. That is the diathesis. Check whether any detail is actually a symptom (the outcome). Set those aside. Do not name a trait such as neuroticism unless the scenario gives evidence for it. Suppressed needs, perfectionism, or avoidance can each be the diathesis without neuroticism ever being mentioned.

Students often think: the diathesis is whatever happened most recently in the scenario. Actually: the diathesis is the long-standing vulnerability that was there before the trigger. The most recent, one-time event is usually the stressor. Students often think: if a disorder involves worry, the diathesis must be high neuroticism. Actually: only name a trait the scenario gives evidence for. A long-standing pattern of perfectionism or suppressed needs can be the diathesis without neuroticism being mentioned. Students often think: symptoms such as lost sleep or withdrawal are part of the diathesis or the stressor. Actually: symptoms are the outcome the model is trying to explain. They are neither the diathesis nor the stressor.

1. A student has a long-standing pattern of perfectionistic, rigid standards. Three months after an injury ends her season, she begins compulsively reviewing every detail, searching for what she could have done differently. Identify the diathesis and the stressor. Show answer Diathesis: her long-standing perfectionistic, rigid standards. Stressor: the injury that ended her season. The compulsive reviewing is a symptom, the outcome the model explains. 2. Why can a symptom never be the diathesis? Show answer The diathesis exists before the stressor and helps cause the disorder. A symptom appears after the stressor as part of the disorder itself, so it is the result, not a cause.

items.x: Sadness is a normal, healthy response to loss. MDD is a lasting disturbance in mood and functioning that persists for weeks, and it often includes symptoms that have nothing to do with emotional pain, such as changes in sleep, appetite, and energy. Criterion Description Criterion A Five or more symptoms during the same two-week period, at least one being depressed mood or anhedonia. Criterion B Clinically significant distress or difficulty functioning. Criterion C Not caused by a substance or a medical condition. Duration At least two weeks, and a change from how the person functioned before. Anhedonia is the key distinguishing feature Anhedonia is the loss of interest in, or capacity to feel pleasure from, activities a person used to enjoy. It is not simple disinterest: a person with anhedonia can take part in something they used to love and still feel nothing. This is the most clinically important feature separating MDD from ordinary low mood. High neuroticism is MDD's strongest personality predictor; high agreeableness combined with pushing down one's own needs can also raise vulnerability. Loss can trigger MDD in a vulnerable person, but normal bereavement alone does not meet the criteria.

Not everyone who goes through a trauma develops PTSD. It develops in some trauma survivors, and involves four symptom clusters that last beyond the immediate aftermath. Cluster Description Criterion A: Exposure Experiencing or witnessing a traumatic event, learning that it happened to someone close, or repeated exposure through work, involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or violence. Criterion B: Intrusion Recurring distressing memories, nightmares, flashbacks, or strong body reactions to reminders. Criterion C: Avoidance Avoiding thoughts, feelings, people, places, or conversations linked to the trauma. Criterion D: Negative cognition and mood Distorted blame, persistent negative beliefs, loss of interest, feeling cut off from others, being unable to feel positive emotions. Criterion E: Arousal Irritability, being constantly on guard, a strong startle response, poor sleep, trouble concentrating. Duration: more than one month. Why PTSD's personality links are "more complex" For GAD, OCD, and MDD, one trait direction (usually high neuroticism) is the consistent risk factor. PTSD is less tidy. High neuroticism is a risk factor, but low neuroticism combined with avoidant coping can also raise risk, because pushing distress away can prevent the emotional processing needed to make sense of the event. High conscientiousness can protect or harm, depending on whether it shows up as problem-solving or as rigid suppression of emotion. A lack of social support after the event is one of the strongest risk factors of all.
